utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Good morning, Mr. Kingori.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you for your staying for one more day. Mr. Karadzic, you have an hour today. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good morning, Excellencies. Good morning to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kingori, good morning.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm going to try to go through everything briefly and quickly, the things that we agreed on during our interview. Can I just remind you that you said that you assumed the duties of the head of the team when in early July 1995, the 10th, the 9th, or the 8th of July, when your colleague went to the hospital. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. The -- my colleague went to the hospital much earlier, not on the 10th or 9th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you became the head of the team in early July; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, we can assume I took over the duties of the head of the team around that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know and were you informed that the Muslims or Muslim soldiers very often placed their weapons close to our observation posts and opened fire from there, and that this was something that was the -- a matter of misunderstanding between them and the soldiers of the Dutch Battalion?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, as military observers we did not have any observation posts. They were manned by DutchBat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm thinking about the United Nations. The DutchBat as well as yourselves were members of the United Nations. Did the Dutch soldiers inform you that they had problems with the Muslim side because it was using the presence of the observation posts by using those places as firing locations in order to draw Serb fire?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, they complained about the BiH presence at the OPs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'm talking about the B&H army. Were you informed that the B&H army misused the presence of DutchBat by situating themselves close by and firing from such locations in order to draw out Serbian fire -- I'm sorry, you did say that it was the BH. In the interpretation I got that you said it was the VRS. I apologise. I am satisfied with your answer. There's no need to go over it again. Were you informed that DutchBat was very afraid of the Muslim army close by, that they were prevented from withdrawing, and that they also had fire, to say the least, from the Muslim side and even exchanges of fire?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, there was such an incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you recall that a Dutch soldier was killed, that he was killed by a Muslim fighter?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You informed us that Colonel Vukovic complained to you about helicopter flights and that these helicopters were shipping in weapons and that Becirovic denied that. However, you found out that even Ramiz Becirovic had a helicopter accident and he was hurt, or rather, that this helicopter that he was in was downed, that he was injured in this accident, but that he survived?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, that issue occurred and we were informed by Colonel Vukovic. And later on it's not Becirovic who denied. It was the mayor of the opstina who denied, according to my records, but later on we found that Ramiz was injured.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you receive information about weapons and ammunition being transported in these helicopters?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, this was said to us by Colonel Vukovic, that there were weapons on board, but we could not verify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at 1D04770, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can I ask you to look at this document from May 1995. It's an official report by the command of the 28th Division of the security organ about the event that we're talking about. So this was before the critical events. May I ask you just to look where it says that they had a heliport and that it crashed close to the heliport. Can you look at that, please. Somewhere around line 10, let me just take a look, I think in the English version it's probably on the next page -- actually, it's towards the bottom of the page where it says that they were stored in a facility used for MTS, materiel and technical equipment. You would agree that this is military equipment, this is weapons and ammunition. Did you know that they had a heliport and then next to the heliport they had a warehouse for materiel and technical equipment?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I was not aware.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we look at page 4 of this document, please. Yes, it's the same page in the English as well. If you can look at the last section after the investigating judge ordered the present members of military security to sort out the bags, packages, personal belongings, and so on and so forth. It's noted then what was found next to the helicopter: Pistols; rubber truncheons, 18 pieces; 11 Kalashnikovs; and so on and so forth. Can we look at the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You can see that there are wrist-watches, Motorolas, uniform trousers, all of this is for the 285th Brigade, for the 282nd, 281st Brigade, all of the things that were being transported by the helicopter that crashed. Can we conclude with good reason that not every helicopter was downed and that many of these helicopters could fly without being observed?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, crashing of one helicopter that we had not sighted does not necessarily mean that there were others that passed without being noticed. Because at least the DutchBat could also have seen it. So that is not a direct conclusion. We cannot be able to conclude that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do we agree that this activity was strictly banned in a demilitarised Srebrenica and that it constituted a violation of the agreement and that this was a combat activity, replenishment and shipping in additional weapons. Do we agree that this was not permitted?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I totally agree with you, this was not permitted; so was the activities by the BSA against the Muslims in the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And probably you will be asked this in re-direct by the Prosecution. Did you establish who was the first to violate the agreement, what was the action, and what was the reaction?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I did not establish who violated the VCFA first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Colonel, by the activities by the BSA against the Muslims in the enclave, do you refer to the attack against the enclave or the downing the helicopter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I mean is the continuous activities that were being done against the Muslims in the enclave. That included the firing against them, the shelling of the enclave much earlier before the main onslaught, and also the activities that were carried out during July -- June and July of 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And were these activities against the protected area, the demilitarised area, the civilian area at unprotected targets as -- or as against what the Secretary-General described as an un -- or as a stronghold?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was against the demilitarised area, the civilian area, and anything else that was inside the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Assuming that there were no fighters there, 15.000 of them, 10.000 of whom had reached Tuzla. Is this something that you call a demilitarised zone?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I still refer to it as a demilitarised zone because it was demilitarised and availability of two, three, or whatever number of guns does not mean an area was not demilitarised. It was only that there were few guns and that is not in question. What I know is that -- and we have reported before that there were a few guns available in the enclave, but that does not mean that the area was not demilitarised.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sir, could you please tell us the period during which it was demilitarised, or rather, remilitarised?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know what you mean by that. Because you know when it was demilitarised. You were there when the accord was signed. And it remained like that. Only that we know and it is documented that a few guns here and there could be seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: For the sake of interpretation, could you please specify when you say "a few guns," are you referring to rifles or cannon?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I mean small arms because we have recorded on that, and I think at one instance, I think where we saw or it was reported, that there was a machine-gun that had been sighted. But there were no heavy weapons that were reported about by us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And your assertion that the zone was demilitarised, how does that comport with the position of the United Nations, whose representative you were over there?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, obviously the UN system -- the United Nations knew about what was happening because we were reporting throughout. When we sight a few guns, we could send a report on the same. Whatever we found in the enclave we could report and it was known all over. And you cannot assume that when you demilitarise a place it becomes hundred per cent without a weapon. It's not possible. So that to us was not possible to achieve a hundred per cent proper that you cannot find a gun here or there. And we were complaining -- and especially DutchBat were complaining whenever they were on patrol, when they could see some BiH men with guns, they would complain to the Chief of Staff and they would be told: This is wrong. And that the next time they would be -- the guns would be removed from them. And you remember an incident and I do not want to go down into it because you have not asked about it, but there is an incident whereby the Muslims did not grant the DutchBat permission to go through because they thought they would get demilitarised, the guns they had would be removed from them. So in fact what I'm trying to say is we were passing the information to the UN system every time we could find anything to report on, even on some people with guns in the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'm concerned by your persistent assertions which are absolutely contrary to what is stated in documents of the United Nations. Have you ever seen a report by the UN Secretary-General --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you are not to argue with the witness. When the witness has given his answer, whether you agree with him or not, just get on with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you ever see the UN Secretary-General's report about the fall of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I don't remember seeing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender the report about the helicopter crash.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. I have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 2001, Your Honours. D2001.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at D10965 briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: A little bit earlier you referred to -- you said that you could not draw a conclusion on the basis of one helicopter. Now I would like to show you the final analysis of the operation of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you give the number again.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- of the air-lift regarding -- and the fights -- in and out of Srebrenica. 1D1965.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is it D1965?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Or 1D040723. Can we look at the next page, please. Can we look at the first sentence, please. "Between the 27th of February, 1993, until 7th May 1995 there was an air-lift from the territory of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina to meet the needs of the enclaves of Srebrenica, Zepa, and Gorazde. The main aim of introducing and maintaining the air-lift was to transport and ensure combat equipment, evacuation of wounded, the functioning of the organs of authority ..." And then a little bit lower it says: "Even in spite of the presence of the UNPROFOR, which did not fulfil its mandate to protect the civilian population in territories of the enclaves," and so on and so forth, "morale of the fighters and civilians has improved not only because of the supply of war materiel and -- and war materiel but also because of the reassurance that they have not been abandoned ..." and so on and so forth. Did you know this air-lift was established and that helicopter flights were not accidental but they were a rule?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was not aware of these flights.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I am not going to dwell on this document anymore. It's already been admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at D1039, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a UN document, isn't it. Akashi is writing to Annan -- actually, he's writing to the Secretary-General and is informing Annan and Goulding, and you know who these people are.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is the 26th of January, 1994. Could you please look at item 5.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Actually, can we have the first page to see whether it's the same document. No, this is the 11th of July, 1995. 1D4882. Could we have that, please. I am sorry. I thought it had been admitted. Can we have the second page now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please look at: [In English] "The Bosnian government has taken tactical advantage of the presence of UNPROFOR beyond the stated objectives of the relevant Security Council Resolutions. The establishment of safe areas in spring last year was designed to stop any further Bosnian Serb advances. While this objective has been achieved by UNPROFOR's presence, the Bosnian Muslim forces have recently embarked on an increasingly offensive approach, partly using the safe areas" -- next page - "as a staging ground. For the Bosnian Serbs this is a cause of great concern which has led them to question UNPROFOR's impartiality increasingly. In the political preparations for the two operations, therefore, it has to be kept in mind that the situation has changed as regards Security Council Resolutions 836 and 844." [Interpretation] So already in January 1994 it was clear that the presence of the United Nations had been abused and you knew nothing of that; right?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Really, when you say the position of the United Nations has been abused, Your Honour, I don't understand by who. Because for sure both sides had their own reasons to assume that the United Nations was not working for their cause. The Muslims were feeling the same because they thought UNPROFOR was there to protect them, but they were still being attacked throughout. And obviously to them they felt the UN is a -- has abandoned them. So even if the BSA could have felt or the Bosnian Serbs could have felt the same, really it's an issue of who says what first. Because I'm sure there are other areas where they -- the Muslims have complained about the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sir, let us see what it is that the UN thinks, not the Serbs or the Muslims. The first objective is to stop the Serbs from advancing; that has been achieved. The second objective was not achieved. Rather, the presence of the UN has been abused --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: -- in order to have the Serbs attacked from there. Did you know of this official position of the UN?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I think Mr. Karadzic understood what I was about to say and reverted to a question. But I think we're going down that same lane again of statement after statement after statement only to conclude with a small question and I ask that it stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please bear in mind how and what to put to the witness. Do not make a statement, as indicated by Ms. West. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The interest of the Defence is to show that this witness speaks of things --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- that he does not know anything about, that he a partial --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- no, then -- put your question then. Otherwise you lead us to question your ability to represent yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kingori, my question was not what the Serbs and Muslims think, but rather what the UN thinks, what your bosses think. Did you know that this truth had already been established in January 1994?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was not aware of this letter. I've never seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We object. This cannot go to the witness's credibility. It's from January of 1994.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I respond?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This witness continuously served the UN. It was his duty to know what he was coming to do and where he was coming to serve. He absolutely had to be aware of this, and he should be confronted with this knowledge that his institution had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber agrees with Ms. West's observation. We will not admit this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kingori, I asked you whether you knew that I had stopped the Serb activity around Srebrenica in 1993. Now I would like you to have a look at a document from that period, 1D4774 [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, could you kindly repeat the number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D04974.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm being told that it hasn't been released.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe later, then. Before the end. Let us go back to our interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You confirmed to us and I see that this is contained in your statement in paragraph 3 that you knew that there were forward air controllers, courageous young men, well equipped, who forwarded NATO aircraft. They worked for NATO; right?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I didn't say -- I'm not very sure who they worked for, but I know they were British and they were inside the enclave and maybe they could assist as air -- forward air controllers on aircrafts that were being used by NATO. I didn't say they were working for NATO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: 131. Could you please have a look at that paragraph of your statement, 131. Whose aircraft were being guided, Mr. Kingori?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were NATO aircrafts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That is what you speak of in paragraph 131; right?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I speak about. But that does not mean that they were employed by NATO. They could have been employed by maybe the British government or whatever, just only that they assisted the NATO. So I'm not sure about all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that the overall presence of international organisations required our consent. Did we ever give our consent for the presence of forward air controllers?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you see any killing in Srebrenica during those critical days?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know what you mean, but if you were talking about directly someone shooting at somebody, I did not witness that. But at least I saw people who had been killed by the bombardment that was staged by the BSA on Srebrenica. I witnessed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you investigate any incidents that resulted in death?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and it is on record and we relayed the same to the UN headquarters. And I remember even one had been killed by shrapnels and we reported exactly like that because we had to check all the bodies so that we could determine what had killed an individual. If it was just injuries, we could check what could have injured that person before taking them to the hospital. So we were investigating all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you investigate any other incidents that resulted in death?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know like which ones you may mean maybe -- you are meaning. I am not very sure what you mean by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In your vicinity in Potocari, were there any incidents that resulted in death that you had investigated or reported on?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. There are some people who died. I think there is one woman who died inside the hospital I think trying to deliver or something like that and we reported on that. There is somebody who tried to kill himself; we reported on that. There were several other incidents that we were reporting on. Whatever we could see or hear we were reporting on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When was the first time that you learned that there had been killings in Srebrenica? During the interview you told us that you found out about that much, much later and that you were very surprised because you had expected people to be taken to Tuzla. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't understand the whole question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We asked you when it was that you first learned that there had been such killings that this trial is dealing with, or rather, these executions. When did you first learn of that? Did you know of that when you were there or is what you told us during the interview correct, that you found out about that much, much later when you returned to Kenya and you were very, very surprised?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I know is that -- and exactly what I told you was that the mass killings that occurred to the men of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Muslims who were killed, I learnt about it much later. But for sure there were doubts on as to the whereabouts, the location, of these men after they left the enclave. All those doubts were there and is reported that their destiny could not be established. We did not know whether they would be killed or not and we were praying and hoping for the best. That is now on those mass killings. But on the bombardment and killing of the Muslims inside the enclave, obviously I was there and I witnessed most of the occurrences.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us specifically who you meant? In your view, who was it that was killed? The people who were seen off on those buses going to Kladanj? Who are the persons who fell victim?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I know and what I believe is that from the initial phase of separating the men from the women and children, there could have been a deliberate plan to eliminate those men. And I still believe those are the men -- the ones who were put in a separate house, the ones who were put in different buses from their families are the ones who could have been killed or exterminated elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So those you considered to be civilians, those who went to Kladanj, you do not think that they were the ones who were the victims. Rather, you think that it was those who you say were treated as POWs. They were lined up and so on. Those who were at the white house; right?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: If I could just make a clarification. I don't believe that the witness indicated that they were treated as POWs. He just described them as the men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I expected the same from the witness. Could you put your question again.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in his statement the witness said that they treated them in the following way. They lined them up and so on and so forth. They took away their personal property and they treated them like prisoners of war. That is in his statement and I'm going to find the exact place.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. I was just going to ask that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 173, paragraph 173.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Where did Mr. Kingori say that they were prisoners of war or treated as such? Yes, I see it, "like they were prisoners of war." Yes, what is your question, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: My question, Mr. Kingori: You think that the persons that the Serb soldiers were treating as POWs were the one who fell victim, the ones who boarded buses, et cetera, those are the ones you mean; right? Or are you referring to the civilians who boarded buses that were going to Kladanj and were evacuated in that way?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, the people, according to me, that I think were exterminated that way are the ones who were taken by buses from Srebrenica -- from Potocari. Those who had been separated from their families and kept in a white house, taken in different buses from their families, are the ones who were exterminated. These are not prisoners of war. These were men who were picked from their families. These are men who were picked from their families.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How do you know that they were not part of the 28th Division, that they were not combatants, and that many of the Serb soldiers from the surrounding area did not know about their activities? Did you establish that they were not combatants?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I did not establish that. But it's good to know that at that time most of the soldiers were in the field. Most of those people who had arms were in the field. Of course, you cannot miss one or two being inside there, and that is why General Mladic, when he was going through a list and checking all the men inside DutchBat compound who had been injured, was checking through that list to confirm whether any of them could have been in their list of soldiers. But the ones outside there are the ones -- are the men who were outside in the white house were separated from their families. So I don't see the connection there, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What list did you refer to, Mladic went through a list?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't mean General Mladic and I'm sorry for that. I meant Major Nikolic. Major Nikolic is the one who had a list and who was checking those who had been taken to DutchBat hospital with -- you know, checking all those who were injured against the list that he had, to confirm whether they were soldiers or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Or alleged criminals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, or alleged criminals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How many people were in the white house then?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I cannot remember -- I do not know the actually number, but there were many, there were many I believe, there were very many.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's difficult for me to give an actual number, but I know there are many -- there were many. And we could see that because some were below, you know, the base -- the basement. Others were on top. Some were, you know -- they were huddled properly inside -- sandwiched, they were sandwiched, they were sort of pressed against each other. There were very many of them inside that building.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kingori, we saw that they stood on a terrace following what was happening. We saw that on a film that was shown here. Are those the people who were packed as sardines? We saw a picture of the white house, people were standing on the terrace, behind the regular railing or fence on the terrace. They did not allow you to enter the white house; right?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, Your Honour, those are two questions and I'll answer both. One of them is on those who could be seen at the house at the terrace, obviously those were not enjoying a picnic. You could see they were huddled together and those are the ones who were slightly better because they were on top. The others who were below them on the lower floor, there were many who were there. And I could see them -- from outside I could see them and even the film can show just a little bit of it. But those who were below were not captured by the video. And I saw all of them and I could actually establish that they were not having fun inside there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. All right, Mr. Kingori, you say that you singled out some young boys, saved them, et cetera. So you did have this authority vis-a-vis the Army of Republika Srpska. You could single out these people, like this man is not going, or rather, this boy is only 14 and so on and so forth. And you said that the people who were there were between the ages of 16 and 60; right?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, besides being a military observer, I'm a human being. I could be able to see that some of these boys who were being taken like they were of fighting age just because their sizes could show that they're slightly big actually did not qualify them to be actually of fighting age or to be soldiers or to be perceived like they were soldiers. They were very young, naive. You know, they were people you could see who do not know anything about the war you are talking about. So when you see them being removed and you, you know -- obviously we knew the consequences of those boys, those men, being taken to a different place. Really, we -- I could not just stand by and watch that happening, and that is why I ensured that the ones who were near where I was I could just remove them -- actually ask them, "What is your age?" When he says 12, 13, 14, or whatever, I would say, "No, no, take him back" and follow and ensure that he goes back to the buses with their families. And as is documented, immediately I could turn and do other things or follow the route, I would find the same boys -- some of those boys had been taken back, but obviously I saved a few. What I'm saying is I had no interest in either the Muslims or the Serbs. I was interested in making sure that at least these boys are not harmed because they were not of fighting age. They were not soldiers at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I am grateful to you for each and every one that you had singled out. However, my point is that you were respected by the Army of Republika Srpska and that they did what you asked them to do. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, you're wrong. You're very wrong on that, in that I was not doing anything for either side. It's documented that I was respected or the UNMOs were respected from both sides of the divide, from the BSA side and from the Muslim side, we were respected because we were neutral. So seeing this happening and telling them, the boys -- you know, saving the boys does not mean that I was working for the Muslims. I was not at all. And actually, it would be wrong to assume that I was working for any of those sides because I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: My question probably was not clear to you. I thanked you for saving them, but my point was that you did have that option, that the Serbian soldiers did listen to you. If you said, "This young man is not going there," in that case they obeyed you. I mean, you did manage to do what you did; right?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you listen to me properly I said at that particular moment they could agree and let the boys leave, but immediately I turned and walked towards a certain direction, some of them could be removed, meaning they were not that -- as obedient as you are trying to put it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at 1D04974 for a second, please. This should already be uploaded into e-court. I'm sorry for not referring to it in advance, but I feel that I need to show it because of two paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You can see that this is a report on the meeting between General Mladic -- actually, on the meeting of UNPROFOR soldiers separately with General Mladic and then General Halilovic. And then they refer to some ammunition that was found, what Mladic requested.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And can we look at the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mladic says here that NATO planes should not fly low and then in the second paragraph that Serbs are ready to negotiate and to resolve any problems by political means. Then in paragraph 5 that Mladic said that he could have taken Srebrenica whenever he wanted to but he didn't wish to do that, that he wanted a political solution. And then in the fourth paragraph that he would refer them to the government and the parliament of Republika Srpska for all political matters. And then one paragraph but last, where it says that after Mladic they also spoke to Halilovic, and Halilovic said: [In English] "He went to -- on to say that if Srebrenica fell, chaos would follow since the population would attempt to take revenge." [Interpretation] Already in 1993 it was clear there were atrocities committed on all sides and that if the Serbs were to return, the population would retaliate, and he did not accuse the army but the population of retaliating. And then in the last paragraph he said that he would attend meetings if the offensive were to be halted. And I halted the offensive and I banned any kind of investigations because they would lead to revenge. Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, you mentioned that on Monday when we met, but for sure this was April 1993 and it's good that you stopped that fight at that time. But I also wish you did the same in 1995, to save the enclave and the people therein.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether we have a basis to admit this through this witness. Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I object to the admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For the same reason, we'll not admit this, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kingori, there is one thing that is quite confusing to me, it's causing confusion.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 1D04784, please. There should be a translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting for the translation, this is an intercepted conversation intercepted by the Muslim state security from Tuzla on the 16th of July, and General Mladic here informs about me reporting to Tolimir, Toso, how Karisik, the police commander, informed me that Pandurevic agreed the passage of these Muslims to their territory. And then Mladic says: I am -- since I have nothing to do with him -- asked the duty officers to urgently make the connection. Did you know that we opened the corridor and enabled the passage of civilians and a number of the fighters through our territory, in spite of battles that went on until the 16th? We enabled them to pass through.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, the thing I knew was that the -- according to the document you showed yesterday, they fought their way out of the enclave. But it could also have been to your interest to give them safe passage so that you don't encounter a lot of problems. In fact, it could have been better for them to leave the enclave to you because that is how initially from the starting of the war that is what the BSA wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sir, I am not asking you about motives but about facts. Did you know that in spite of major casualties, both on the Serbian and the Muslim side, and in spite of ongoing fighting, the corridor was opened for the column to pass through? Because a little bit earlier you said that I should have done something to save the enclave in 1995, like I did in 1993. And here is the answer. Even though there were fighters and it was a legitimate target and even though there were many casualties on the Serb side on this route, ultimately we did open up the corridor for them to pass through, whereas the buses went on their own route. We're talking about combat breakthrough here. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I said that really it was to your interest that you allow them to leave, that you give them a route out, not necessarily a safe one, but at least a route out. If you press somebody towards a certain place, really, and you want them out of your way, you give them an escape route and you did exactly that, the same way that you provided buses for the others who had been brought all the way up to Potocari to leave the enclave, not telling them to stay so that you could live together in harmony or looking for a political solution, but to make sure that they get out of the enclave. So to achieve -- that was meant to achieve your initial objective.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sir, now you are behaving partially and as the Prosecutor. This is not for you to say, but let us go back to the buses --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know the contents of the two meetings?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's time to conclude. You put your last question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would just like to cover one last topic and there will be two or three additional questions. Do you know about the meeting between Karremans and Mladic, two meetings in the evening of the 11th of July?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I heard about those meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know the content of the meetings? Do you know that Karremans came and said that he was given an assignment, he was asked to ask the Serbian side to permit the evacuation of civilians?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the Serbian side didn't have anything prepared and that the Serbian side had asked for buses from the United Nations and that they got the reply that they didn't have buses but that they would provide fuel?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was not aware of that. What I was aware of is that we requested that the UN brings buses to pick the Muslims from the enclave, that is, from the Potocari area out to Tuzla. And General Mladic said no. He's the one who is going to provide buses. And it is all documented.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sir, you spoke about that with Mladic on the 12th of July, but on the 11th, in the evening, Karremans convinced Mladic that the United Nations did not have buses. Who authorised you? Who promised and who said that the United Nations did have buses? Which of your bosses did that?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would object to a misstatement of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, you would like to have the reference if --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Well, I'm objecting to the word "convinced," but I think that's inaccurate -- an inaccurate description of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Hmm.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mladic was told in the evening of the 11th of July that the United Nations did not have buses, so he took it upon himself to secure the buses. And on the 12th that is what he did. However, on the 12th of July, you offered buses to him. In whose name? If Karremans says that there were no buses, what were the buses that you were counting on then?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, we had requested through our normal channels for buses to be brought so that they could be able to evacuate the Muslims from the enclave and they were told that that could be organised and that is what I told General Ratko Mladic, I told him about the same. But later on -- immediately he said, "No, I have organised my own transport and it is the one that is going to take these people outside the enclave. I don't need the UN."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But who told you that the United Nations had buses when Karremans said that they did not? Who was it who told you that they did have them?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think we may dwell on this for a long, long time. But for sure, if Karremans had requested through his channels, through UNPROFOR, and I requested through military observers, these are two different channels. I don't mean that it doesn't go to the same place. It could have eventually have gone to the logistics side. Maybe he had the good answer of -- that the UN does not have buses. Or maybe I had a good answer that they are going to send buses. But for sure General Mladic told me openly that he does not need the UN buses. So it really does not matter whether Karremans had assured -- had told General Mladic that he had no buses. It really does not matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Kingori, you said you had "requested through our normal channels for buses to be brought." When did you make that request and specifically when?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we called that morning and said that the humanitarian catastrophe -- not catastrophe, the humanitarian situation in the enclave --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: "That morning" being 12th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The morning of 12th. We had said: Up to now we need people to be removed from the enclave, the Muslims who are inside there, and that included the whole lot even of us. And I was told that the UN would send buses. They did not say when --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So who, specifically who do you mean by the UN?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The military observer command chain because I talked to our sector --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Sector North-east?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sector North-east.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those are the ones I requested. So -- and I was assured that there would be a transport but they didn't say when. But then immediately I told that to General Ratko Mladic. He said he does not need the UN, he is going to provide buses. And within a very short time the buses were available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kingori, there's another thing that concerns me. That whole day Mladic was accompanied by journalists and TV cameras. I had the opportunity to ask Mladic. He remembers you but he claims that you did not even exchange a single sentence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, please call Mladic for your Defence witness. The witness has answered that question. I think you --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But the question is: You had spent a half an hour with him once, and then the second time, how many minutes did you spend with him?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, the second session with General Mladic did not take long. We didn't stay much with him, but the first one took a bit long time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can I tender this intercept, please? 1D04784.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: There is an English translation of that and it's a duplicate of 65 ter 31129A, so maybe you can just admit that one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But do we have a basis to admit this? You do not object to --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I don't object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You do not object to it. Can we upload it before we admit it. I would like to see it. English translation as well. Mr. Karadzic, when you asked the witness that you -- "we opened the corridor for the column," what did you mean by "we"?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellency, I was informed by a policeman and asked for my approval to support Pandurevic to open the corridor. I called Tolimir. Tolimir called Mladic and Mladic sent a telegram on the matter. Here this is all being described. We, the Serbs - not I personally, but I did support and protect the back of Pandurevic to open it up so that the people can pass through. There was an entire set of communication between Pandurevic and the Muslim commander from Tuzla to secure that there are no clashes so that they could pass through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Given the position of the Prosecution, we'll admit this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D2002, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just conclude.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kingori, I'm sorry that I had to be specific about many things.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And for the transcript, I have to tell the Trial Chamber that there are plenty of paragraphs left that the Defence would have needed to dwell on and to clarify but did not have time to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Kingori, I just want to go back to about a half an hour ago when we were speaking about prisoners of war and we looked at your amalgamated statement, particularly we're looking at paragraph 173, where it says, it's short: "When the men were being taken to the buses, they were not allowed to go back and pick up their belongings. They were being put in the buses without their belongings, without the items that they were forced to leave out there. They were taken towards the buses one by one, like they were prisoners of war, one by one, one following each other, with no space in between, and the soldiers everywhere." Sir, my question for you is: Did you use the term "prisoners of war" in here because of what you visually saw, this formation line?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's very clear from what I've written here that that these to me were normal civilians, normal Muslims, inside the enclave, normal men who had been separated from their families. And right now they're being forced to enter buses to go to destinations they did not know without their belongings and other items, like identification, that they had left outside. And then they were being taken like they were prisoners of war, one by one, following each other, and being closely guarded like they were POWs. That does not mean that they were prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And the following paragraph, 174, speaks about their identifications. In your experience, is it customary with prisoners of war to take their identifications from them?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's illegal to remove identification cards, identification tags, from an individual. It's wrong. Because eventually you may not be able to identify who that particular person was.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, may we go into private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just ask -- I'm sorry. I thought that it was finished.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir we're going to -- if we can go to 65 ter 23109A. And this is an MSF document. We're looking at page ending in 6146. And for ease of reference, Colonel, I put this in front of you in hard copy because I thought it would be faster. And we're looking at the one that says 6146. This is a document that's dated July 9th. Now, on July 9th, was that the day that you left Srebrenica --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that is the time we left Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We didn't hear you, Mr. Karadzic. You would like to see the page? Yes, it's coming.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Now I have it. Thanks. Sorry, I have it now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So that is the day that you left, but there was a period of time where you were still in Srebrenica that day. Can you describe the shelling going on?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, we were there from morning up to later in the afternoon and the shelling was continuous, heavy shelling. And it was centred mainly in the town of Srebrenica and other outlying towns.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And so in this document we see at the first line, this is from the woman at MSF: "Heavy shelling continuously over the day, mostly in the town ..." And is that consistent with your memory as well?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I want to go down a little bit where it says: "The president has a meeting now with opstina where they will decide what to do ..." Where she here refers to the president, is that the person to whom you, I think, referred to as the mayor, Mr. Suljic?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, this is Osman Suljic.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And yesterday when you were shown document P4150 by Mr. Karadzic, and that's when you made your comments, this is in fact the same person?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: She writes: "UNHCR asked the president if a request for evacuation of the population should be done. Not yet was the answer ..." Colonel, when you were describing that letter from Mr. Suljic as not being taken in isolation, I'll ask you this: Does it surprise you that at this point he had not yet asked for an evacuation?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, it just confirms what I had said, that by that time it had not been made.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'm going to refer you to yesterday's transcript, 22893 and 94. At that point Mr. Karadzic said: "Do you know that both Doctors Without Borders and UNPROFOR reported that Serbs were not hitting buildings or features but they were firing around to prevent movement, so-called barrage fire to prevent movement?" Do you remember that question, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And I would like to refer you now to what's marked 6156. And in e-court I think it's page 3 of this document. Yes, it's on the screen now. This is an MSF document from the 10th of July. And here MSF writes: "The hospital is totally overcrowded ..." She goes on: "According to people coming from the centre we can expect plenty of wounded." And then a little bit further below she says: "I stated very clearly that I want to have a neutral zone so it cannot be a target," and here she's talking about the hospital. Was it your understanding on the 10th of July that at this point it was MSF's position that she did not want security at the hospital so it would not be a target?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, hospitals internationally are not supposed to be targeted, but if there are soldiers or there is an armoury or something that can attract bombardment from the other side, it would be dangerous for those who are sick and being treated in the hospital. So I agree with MSF that there was a need to maintain neutrality, not to have soldiers guarding the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And if we can go to 6157, which in e-court will be page 4. This is the same day a little bit later in which she is writing to a captain, she says: "I have to inform you about the fact that now the surrounding of the hospital and our house are being targeted by the shells." "... for us it's not possible anymore to move out of the shelter." Sir, is this consistent with the information that you had as well?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, this clearly confirms what I had said, that the hospital had been targeted and that it was easy for us to identify a place which was being targeted.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now I would like to go to e-court --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For what and --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness is redefining the question. The Prosecutor's question was: Is it correct that the area surrounding the hospital became a target, whereas the witness says the hospital became a target. The surrounding area is different from the hospital itself. It's the kind of gun-fire that does not imply anyone moving around.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The documents are there and the witness answered as far as he can. So I don't understand the objection.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, the objection is the fact that the question is being redefined. It's not the hospital that was being targeted but the surrounding area. That was the question. It was a question of barrage fire, them not being able to move around.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Your objection is overruled. Let's continue, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'm directing you to yesterday at 22904, Mr. Karadzic was asking you questions about some of the reports that you had written, and in particular you had written that the BSA was being hostile. And he was suggesting that you were using language unfairly with the Serbs. And his question was: "... so you vilify the Serbs that no one else who is in the same places as you were never wrote anything remotely similar or said anything remotely similar. That's why I'm challenging your entire statement. Why did this lady," he meant the MSF lady, "not describe these drastic threats," for example, "issued to old women, people saying that they would be killed?" So I want to talk about this issue of whether other organisations were reporting the activities that you described as hostile by the BSA. We're going to look at 6180, which is I believe e-court page 5 of this exhibit. This is another document from MSF. This is on the 13th of July. "Just coming from the empty camp. It is 4.00 p.m. and all the people are evacuated. We have taken into charge plenty old people who cannot walk and have together with the UN transported them here." Is that reference in regard to the trip that you took to Srebrenica with MSF?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. She's referring to that trip.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: "I see BSA beatings and harassing a crazy man. Horror." Sir, would you agree that your reporting of these hostile incidents that you saw, at least in this case seems to be reported by another organisation as well?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it's quite evident.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I do not follow, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is now manipulation on the part of the Prosecutor. We saw that in Prijedor a man was killed, a man who was insane, but I was speaking to Mr. Kingori about this statement to the effect that an old lady was being mistreated in a hospital and the MSF said something else. I objected to something different from what the Prosecutor is saying now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The grounds were completely different for this claim.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would just point out on the record I did read that particular part, but you will remember right before that the accused referenced specifically paragraph 184, 185 and 186 on how you smeared Serbian soldiers. You say: "... they threatened old women and you use a euphemism when you say 'a bit hostile,' 'that was a bit hostile.'" I would suggest that what he was saying was general and we're not specifically talking about this old woman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I find the line of redirect absolutely legitimate. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would tender those four documents in that 65 ter number and I would ask that they be tendered under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we add that part to the previous one or shall we admit it as a separate document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I thought this -- part of the same document had been already admitted as Defence exhibit. It was my mistake. We'll admit this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P4166, under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. May we go into open session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had objected to this manipulation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. Your terminology of "manipulation" is not acceptable, Mr. Karadzic. Yes, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, is it time for a break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How long would you need to conclude?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I think as a result of today's examination, I would at least need another ten minutes or so, or 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then we'll take a break.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That should be okay with your travel plan, Mr. Kingori?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's okay with me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll take a break for half an hour and resume at ten past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, over the break, I streamlined my questions. So I'm sorry, but my 10- to 15-minute estimate is now much shorter. May we have P02276 [Realtime transcript read in error "P02267"].

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Colonel, yesterday at transcript 22909, Mr. Karadzic asked you this: "And do you know, Mr. Kingori, that the United Nations and the Muslim side already on the 10th knew that the Serbs do not have a decision to the effect that they would enter Srebrenica? On the 10th of July, the Serbs do not intend to go into Srebrenica and yet all of the intercepts and all of the reports showed that?" Do you remember being asked that question?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So you were asked what the UN and the Muslims thought about the Serb decision regarding entering Srebrenica. I'd like to look at what the Serbs were saying even before the 10th. And if you see this document before you, it's dated 9th --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Exhibit Number is 2276 not 67.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: 2276, yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: It's dated the 9th, it's from General Tolimir and it's to the Drina Corps, the President of Republika Srpska, for information. It says: "The president of Republika Srpska has been informed of the successful combat operations around Srebrenica by units of the Drina Corps and that they have achieved results which enabled them to occupy the very town of Srebrenica." Colonel, on the 9th of July, when this was written, is this -- are these words consistent with your observations that the Serbs were on their way in?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it is very consistent and remembering that that is the day we left Srebrenica for Potocari, it was evident that they were coming in in an infantry way, meaning that is after having finished softening the whole target.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: It goes on to say: "The president of the republic is satisfied with the results of combat operations around Srebrenica and has agreed with the continuation of operations for the take-over of Srebrenica, disarming of Muslim terrorist gangs, and complete demilitarisation of the Srebrenica enclave." So, sir, after the 9th and beginning on the -- or this is dated the 9th and those days after, did this -- those combat operations continue?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is true the combat operations continued in the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May I have 65 ter 19553, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Colonel, at 22899 transcript page, the accused in a question said: "I did not say that you were useless, sir. It was the highest commanders of the UNPROFOR who said that military observers were useless." I'd like to show you a report done by NIOD, this is, done by the Dutch military, and it's before you now, and I'd like to go to page 3 of the English and look at their comments and I'll ask you something afterwards. It's a paragraph that begins with "The one UNMO ..." "The one UNMO who appears to have been most active in those days after the fall was the Kenyan Major J. Kingori. He could, in fact, be seen in the film images made on July 12th after the entry of the Serb troops and Mladic. He was also the one who asked him why the men were being separated. At Franken's request he watched the white house on July 13th to check whether the number of men who were led in corresponded with the number who came out. And as DutchBat soldier Karremans wrote in his diary, Kingori also protested continually against the brutal manner in which people were packed together in the buses." Colonel, do you agree with these comments that are made here?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wholly agree with the observations made here and all these comments.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'd now like to go to 65 ter 3991.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now I'd like to look at comments regarding your job activities made by your own superiors. This is July 9th and it's to the military observers in Srebrenica and it's from the CMO. Can you tell us what CMO means?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, CMO means chief military observer. That was the head of the military mission in former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: The subject is "Congratulations." "I would like to pass on my sincerest congratulations to UNMO Srebrenica for your timely and detailed reports. Given the circumstances you are under this is a commendable achievement. The information you produced on 8 July ... was of the highest order and was noted in the forum of the Force Commanders conference 9 July ... by the Chief of Staff who remarked on the 'content and accuracy of the UNMO Srebrenica report.' "I wish you to endeavour to maintain your excellent standards of work, and above all else, stay safe ..." Colonel, do you remember receiving these remarks from your superiors?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't have any more questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. You are not tendering those two documents?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'm not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Then that concludes your evidence, Mr. Kingori. Colonel, on behalf of this Chamber as well as the Tribunal as a whole, I would like to thank you for your coming to The Hague again to give it. Now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So you will be calling the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. The Prosecution calls Paul Groenewegen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And if I can -- for the record, two days ago, on January 11th, you asked us to take Colonel Kingori's diary. We did that. We had it rescanned to a more legible version. It was provided to Mr. Karadzic, and it's P4140.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. While the next witness is being brought in, there's one matter I'd like to deal with. I note that Mr. Tieger is not here, but I take it Madam Uertz-Retzlaff can take care of this. The Chamber -- but it's my -- this is only related to the Defence, however. The Chamber is seized of the accused's motion to compel inspection of items, material to the Sarajevo Defence case filed publicly with a confidential annex on 28th of October, 2011, in which the accused requests pursuant to Rule 66(B) that the Chamber compel inspection of four categories of materials relating to 201 prospective Defence witnesses that may be called in the Sarajevo component of his Defence case. As part of its assessment of the motion and as noted in Appeals Chamber decisions, such as the Bagosora decision on interlocutory appeal relating to disclosure under Rule 66(B) of the Tribunal's Rules of Procedure and Evidence, issued on 25 September 2006, the Chamber examines whether the accused has demonstrated prima facie that the requested items are in the custody or control of the Prosecutor, in particular in cases where the Prosecution challenges the custody or the control of the material sought. In the Prosecution's response to the motion to compel inspection of items material to the Sarajevo Defence case filed publicly with the confidential annexes on 10th of November, 2011, the Prosecution contends that the accused provides no basis to conclude that the vast array of requested material is in the Prosecution's possession, and thus is engaging in a speculative approach with regard to the third prong of this test.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber also notes that the accused's submission lacks any showing in this regard. Before the Chamber rules on the motion, I thus wish to inquire with the Defence if it can clarify on which basis it considers that it has demonstrated prima facie that such categories of items relating to these protected Sarajevo witnesses are in the custody or control of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, would you like us to do that in writing or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll do that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir, for your patience. Would the witness kindly take the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hereby state that I will tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Groenewegen. Would you make yourself comfortable, please. Yes, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. May we have 65 ter 90300, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Can you tell me your name.

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Paul Groenewegen.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, you've testified in the Blagojevic case in 2003; the Popovic case in 2006; and the Tolimir case in 2010. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: An amalgamated statement was prepared containing relevant portions of your prior testimonies, and this is a statement which you reviewed and signed on the 11th of November, 2010. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And is this the statement that you see on the screen before you?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Can you confirm that the statement accurately reflects an amalgamation of the testimonies that you've previously given?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, and if you were asked today about the same matters contained in the statement, would you provide the same information to the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would tender the statement. There are also eight associated exhibits. Of the eight, there are three we do not tender. I will recite the three numbers. 65 ter 19529, 65 ter 40582, and 65 ter 02700, as that was admitted previously by an earlier witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll admit them all. In the meantime, could we upload 65 ter number 2648. I'm not sure we are able to see the markings the witness allegedly made on the map.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I -- it was my understanding, Mr. President, that he pointed out the two OPs on this map which are already marked, the M and the N, but we can have him -- I can address that with him directly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. And at first I'd like to read a summary.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please read out slowly for the sake of the interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So 2648 will not be admitted as an associated exhibit. You will deal with it --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- directly. Yes. But shall we give the number at least for the -- for his 92 ter statement.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P4167, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. The witness first enlisted in the Dutch army as a private in January 1994. He served continuously from that time until December 2003.
