As part of his military service, he was posted in Potocari from January to July 1995. His main duty during that time was to patrol the area. The purpose of these patrols was to ensure that the cease-fire was respected by both sides. During the first months of his assignment, he witnessed military activity between the VRS and the BiH, including fire exchanges and some explosions. He also saw a BiH military presence in the form of men, small-calibre weapons within the enclave. They appeared to him as civilians, attempting to protect the enclave, rather than an organised military unit. DutchBat soldiers were tasked with disarming the BiH. They very rarely saw armed men within the enclave. Though he learned after leaving the region that the BiH army sometimes left the demilitarised zone to take certain actions, he never witnessed this at the time. The witness was stationed at OP Mike in early July, when VRS soldiers began to fire at the Dutch with small- and large-calibre weapons and mortar shells. There was no communication between VRS forces and DutchBat even though he could see them from the OP. Communication with other DutchBat soldiers confirmed that other OPs were also under attack during the same period. The witness interpreted these VRS actions as provocation rather than an attempt to harm DutchBat soldiers, since the shootings did not hit their targets. The witness returned to Potocari on 10 July as part of his regular rotation. DutchBat soldiers there were tense because they expected some VRS action to take place imminently. Early the next morning, refugees began to arrive from Srebrenica, mostly on foot. They seemed very afraid. The DutchBat soldiers were tasked with ensuring that the refugees would make it safely to the compound. Refugees continued to arrive throughout the day, and by the evening of 11 July, thousands were in Potocari, inside and outside the UN compound. There were women, children, elderly men, and not enough food or blankets to provide them. VRS soldiers approached Potocari from the north during the day of July 12th. Some units had dogs. Other VRS troops approached through the hills and the witness saw houses burning on their path, first from the direction of OP Papa, then continuously closer to Potocari. The houses burned in a wave. Following the first troops, the infantry came in and then other groups with cameras and sound reporting and officers who appeared to be acting in co-ordination with the earlier group. DutchBat soldiers created a buffer zone to protect the refugees from VRS soldiers who were approaching them aggressively. Bread trucks and a crew from Serbian television arrived. Bread was distributed to the refugees in what appeared to be a propaganda stunt. The witness learned that the refugees were to be taken out of Potocari and buses later arrived to transport them. First to board the buses were those who wanted to leave. When refugees who did not wish to be transported refused to get on the buses, the VRS initially shouted at them, but then ultimately violence was used to get the refugees onto the buses. The Dutch soldiers attempted to intervene but were ineffective because of the language barrier and confusion. Only women, children, and elderly men were being transported, as the men had already been separated. The witness believed that the women and children had not gone to Potocari of their own free will. The witness believed that they had no other option. The transportation of refugees continued throughout the day, and the witness estimates that thousands of refugees were forced on the buses that day. There were some men present at Potocari. Serb soldiers separated them from their families before the women and children were led to the buses. These hundreds of men were taken to an empty house. These men were aged between 16 and 60 years. The refugees that remained overnight were mostly those who did not want to leave and they were very fearful. The transportation of refugees continued the next day. The witness's role was to ensure that the transportation took place as calmly as possible and to limit aggression on both sides. Serb soldiers continued to separate men from the rest of the refugees. The men were taken to a house, and once the house was full, separate buses came to take them away. He estimates that a few hundred men were separated. The witness saw General Mladic in Potocari on both the 12th and 13th. He was moving through the area with his regular military staff. During the evacuation the witness's attention was drawn to a group of four Serbian soldiers surrounding a Muslim man, four VRS soldiers. The soldiers were wearing camouflage uniforms of various colours without any visible insignia. The witness, however, confirmed that the soldiers all seemed to belong to the Bosnian Serb army, even though they were dressed differently. The soldiers -- the man was dressed as a civilian and did not appear to be armed. The soldiers took him away and forced him to stand facing a wall, and from a distance of about 3 metres, one of them shot him through the back of the head and he collapsed. The witness reported this to his superiors. The witness remained at Potocari until the 20th of July. Your Honour, that concludes my summary. I just have a few questions. May we go into private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. And if we can turn to Sanction. This is 65 ter 2648.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, when you were in Srebrenica you were posted to two different OPs, is that right, observation posts?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: What were the name of those observation posts?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Initially OP Papa and OP November.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And were you ever assigned to another OP as well?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Later on, we handed OP Papa over to another unit and went to OP Mike.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, in front of you is a map and you can see where Srebrenica is located, and there is -- then there is a sort of light purple line that goes around Srebrenica with letters on that line. Do you recognise what that line is?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: This is the enclave with the observation posts.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And at the top of the line as the letters of the alphabet go around we see M -- this is on the northern edge of that line, M, N, O, P. Do those represent where those observation posts were located?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And is it correct, then, that you were assigned at one point to OP Papa, P; OP November, which would be N; and OP Mike, which would be M?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May we tender this, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, this will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P4172, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, in front of you in hard copy you have your statement, your amalgamated statement, and you can refer to it at any time. At this point I'm going to look at paragraph 60 and 61 of your statement. And in that paragraph you described the execution you witnessed. And you said the soldiers who took the civilian man behind the house were all dressed in different sorts of camouflage uniforms, but you nonetheless -- you believed that they were not paramilitaries but that they belonged to the BSA. Can you tell us what it is about what you observed that led you to believe that they all belonged to the BSA?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Different groups were present, of course the very large group of refugees, and they clearly didn't belong to them; and to me, that was the reason to assume that they pertained to the BSA.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: But since they were dressed differently, the soldiers themselves were dressed not all in the same uniform, what was it about the way they behaved that made you believe that they all belonged to the same army and not different armies or different units or organisations?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Because they aggressively took away the person concerned and executed him there.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, Ms. West. By "BSA," Bosnian Serb army, would you include so-called paramilitaries as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wouldn't dare state anything about that, but would you prefer me to describe them as VRS?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: In paragraph 28 of your statement, you mention that on July 12th you remained in what you described as a buffer zone. I'm going to show you some video now, and this is 65 ter 40582. And we're going to start --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And whenever you refer to the trial video, I would appreciate if you could refer to the page number in the transcript in hard copy so that we can follow easily. Transcript of trial video, transcription. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'll do that in a moment, Your Honour. I'm just going to go to another paragraph of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, paragraph 42 of your statement. Thank you. You spoke about -- here you spoke about whether the women and children went to Potocari of their own free will. And you specifically said: "I do not think that the women and children went to Potocari of their own free will, but that they had no other option." Witness, why do you believe that they had no other option?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Well, they were offered the opportunity to leave the area, and of course they would have had the option to stay but this seemed best to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And can you tell us, from what you observed, why it was the best option?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Leaving the area, in my option, was always better than remaining there.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And why was that?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Because the enclave was being overwhelmed, I have to say, by the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And did you see that with your own eyes?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Well, of course I wasn't able to see everything that took place there, but given that the people were that frightened, that's my reason to assume that they didn't come there voluntarily.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may have just one moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We're going to go back to the video. Mr. President, at this very moment we can't locate the transcript but we could play this without any sound because I'm looking for just -- I want him to identify an area and that's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. So we're going to start this video. For the record this is 40582. It's the video V0009035. We're starting at 27.16.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, just follow along in front of you. You can see the video; correct?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Here we're at 27.29. We see an interview with General Mladic. But I'm interested more in the area where the interview takes place. So if we can just keep watching. We're at 27.55 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise this area?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: I recognise this recording.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. And can you tell us, were you there at the time?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: It's not clearly visible on the images, but one of those blue helmets is me.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. And we'll continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: This will continue to play, but is this the buffer zone you spoke about in your statement?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And we can stop there. We're at 28.47.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, what was the purpose of the buffer zone?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: We were informed that we had to set up a line to keep the two parties apart there.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Groenewegen, your evidence given in other Chambers were admitted in an amalgamated form as you heard from Ms. West. And now you'll be further asked by Mr. Karadzic in his cross-examination. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Groenewegen.

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: May I ask you how old you were in 1995? I don't see the year of birth here. You seem very young. How old were you then?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: I was 18 in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And how much military experience did you have at that time?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: One year.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you were there as a private. You didn't have a rank or any special duties; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm a little bit confused in view of the fact that in your statement, or rather, in your testimony of the 10th of July, 2003, on transcript page 1013, I think that's 65 ter 03237; and then in October in a different case, this is IT-05-88-T, on the 5th of October, 2006, on pages 3012 to 13, you said that you were a corporal and that you were a corporal -- I mean, were you a corporal there in January 1994?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: That's not correct. I can't possibly have stated that I was a corporal at the time; but when this first request to testify came, I was a corporal at that time. And that's the source of the confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We clarified that. And this statement from the 29th of September, 1991 [as interpreted], that you gave to the military police, the Dutch military police, representing the Tribunal, was that your first statement that you provided to anyone?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I think that date must be wrong.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Paragraph 3 -- actually, paragraph 5, in the amalgamated statement. And the statement should be 65 ter 19529.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It was noted as 1991 in the transcript. That's why Ms. West rose.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that I did say "1995." I apologise if I did not articulate that clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Before these statements, you had one statement of the 5th of September the same year at your ministry, and then on the 29th of September, a statement to the military police which was asking you questions on behalf of this Tribunal. Before that time, did you provide any other statement?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: In the enclave another statement was drafted. That was the first time I reported this incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: To whom?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: To my immediate supervisor on site.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was this a written statement or report and do you have it?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: I don't have it and it was recorded in writing, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If you do come across it, could you please provide it to us. And if we find it or the OTP, we would like to look at it. In this debriefing of the 5th of September, is it correct that you described some stages during this period? And what I would like to do is to actually check whether this was so. You said that the first stage includes the period of the fall of OP South. Then stage two would be the fall of Srebrenica. Stage three would be receiving and evacuating the local population. And then stage four would be the evacuation of the wounded and the departure of the Dutch Battalion. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: If you read that out to me that way, it rings a bell, but it's been a long time. So if I'm not exactly aware of what I said on which dates and how it read, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. Probably this was divided in order to present the events precisely according to stages, and that's how we will proceed if that is okay with you. You described in paragraph 7 of the amalgamated statement what your duties were. Do you have this statement in front of you?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were supposed to go on patrol and you say here that you were overseeing or monitoring the cease-fire. Do you agree that you were supposed to monitor also the civilian nature of the enclave, that it was secured by somebody before you, and that it was your job to monitor it?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Then this last sentence would need to be corrected: [In English] "The purpose of these border patrols was to see whether there were no conflicts between the two warring parties and to see whether the truce was respected." [Interpretation] Am I correct if I say that it was -- the conflict was frozen -- it wasn't a question of there being a halt to the hostilities and overseeing the truce between the two warring parties, but in fact Srebrenica was demilitarised at the time and that's what the situation was?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Quite honestly, I find this approach a bit confusing regarding the assignment to us at OPs to patrol in the area and to disarm possible parties that might be bearing arms, and this to us concerned primarily the people within the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were aware, thus, that the safe area or the enclave was supposed to have been demilitarised, and if weapons were to appear, you were authorised to confiscate the weapons. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Then you said that it was impossible for the Muslims in the enclave to have weapons pursuant to the agreement. [In English] "It was impossible for them to have weapons due to the agreements." [Interpretation] Would you agree that it would have been better to say it was improper rather than it was impossible?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Can we just have the paragraph number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It was not fully translated, Mr. Karadzic. What paragraph is it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I'm trying to find that now. It states "armies." I'm not sure that this is from this amalgamated statement. I'm going to look for the reference now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you recall saying that, that it was impossible that they had weapons?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: I don't recall any of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If we find the reference, we will show it to you. In paragraph 9 you said that you were aware of the military presence, or rather, of the VRS positions outside the borders of the enclave. Did you ever see the agreement on the demilitarisation and the establishment of the enclave and do you recall that the sequence of steps there was to carry out the complete demilitarisation and then the Serbs would pull their heavy weapons away from the enclaves?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is a very long compound question and if I can just ask Mr. Karadzic to make these questions a bit more simple.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will try.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Paragraph 9 of the amalgamated statement where you say that you were aware of the presence, or rather, the positions of the Army of Republika Srpska outside the borders of the enclave. Did you consider that to be legitimate or illegitimate? Would that be considered a violation of the demilitarisation agreement?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: The situation there was that from our perspective the -- it was just beyond the border from our perspective at the observation post. And as soon as we didn't see any aggressive intentions, we had little control of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And in the same paragraph you say that during the first months, in the beginning, you were not exposed to fire from any side; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now paragraph 10 as well as your testimony in the Blagojevic case on the 10th of July - this is page 1043 - covers the question of what you knew about the military structure of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina in the enclave itself. And then in paragraph 10 you say that to a degree the B&H army did have a presence inside the enclave and that these were small-calibre weapons, that you did not observe - and so on and so forth - weapons of large calibre. And do you agree that they did operate according to the subordination system? You testified to that in the Blagojevic case in 2003. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: So this concerns the hierarchy of the army within the enclave, and as far as I could perceive there was none. At least I never -- I was never able to see any.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you please look at this paragraph 10 of your amalgamated statement. And that's where you say that you agree that they did operate according to the principle of military subordination and organisation. Then you go on to say and you confirmed that in the examination-in-chief today that you understood them to be armed civilians who wanted to defend their enclave. This is my question: Were you aware that the 28th Division existed with four brigades, two independent battalions, and with a 5th Brigade in Zepa, numbering a total of 13- or 14.000 fighters, all of whom perhaps did not have weapons. But if we know that there were shifts, then it's possible that they all could have been armed. Are you aware that there was the 28th Division that had at least four brigades and two independent battalions with a heliport that had regular arms shipments?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: I don't know about this. This is the first time I see this information that you're presenting to me now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you able to have access all over and to see for yourselves that the Muslims or the Muslim army was not concealing anything from you?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: I cannot state anything about that. I never saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you have access to wherever you wanted to check, the tank, the self-propelled gun, the mortars?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't know where the second half of that question came from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have -- well, the second part of the question is based on my thesis that there was the 28th Division with three tanks, at least one self-propelled weapon, mortars of all three calibres --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then you have to put that question first to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the witness said he didn't see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But I'm asking him now if he had access to every part of the enclave in order to see for yourselves that the 28th Division was not concealing anything from you?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: The area where I stayed was from OP Papa to OP Mike, November and the immediate vicinity, and I was basically never in the rest of the enclave and I certainly didn't have free access to all parts of the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And does that mean that you cannot testify about your battalion's experiences but only about your experiences at those two observation posts and about what you yourself saw in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Well, in any case, I can state only about what I saw myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm afraid that your statement contains positions that are broader than those of those two observation posts. Do you know where the Bandera Triangle is located?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Now that you mention this name, I can remember that it was mentioned once; but where it is, I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you informed by your colleagues or commanders that this was a no-go zone for you and that you never actually entered that zone, either you or your colleagues?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: I'm sure we were notified of such at the time, but because we didn't have authority to do any business in the area where I was staying, that's why I paid no further attention to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have map P4172 and can we ask Mr. Groenewegen to look at it and explain some things about the enclave. P4172. Can we zoom in on the lower right-hand corner where we can see the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Groenewegen, did you have any meetings or consultations in the unit? Did you have meetings where you discussed the situation or did you receive any kind of information in writing?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Prior to our deployment in that area, we were briefed once about the overall situation and what the most recent developments had been and that we would be replacing DutchBat II and would remain there for six months.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us what the distance is between Srebrenica proper, the town of Srebrenica, and these lines marking the boundaries of the enclave? Did you know how far the observation posts were from town?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Quite honestly, I cannot state anything about that. It would have been several kilometres, but once again, I was only in the northern part of the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Very well, then. We will determine that on the map. Tell me about this south part, what do these yellow triangles denote?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I've read the answer, but I didn't hear it -- now I can hear it in my earphones. But do we agree, Mr. Groenewegen, that Zeleni Jadar is outside the enclave and that Zepa and Srebrenica are not territorially integrated and this area south of the enclave belongs to the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: When I look at this map, that should be correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that in reality the situation was that the Muslim side unlawfully joined the Zepa and Srebrenica enclaves, cut off our road between Milici and Skelani, made it impossible for us to transport ore, and do you agree that this joining was done unlawfully, illegally?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For -- on what ground, Ms. West?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's a lot of facts in one question of which this -- which this -- at this point this witness is certainly not in a position to answer a question like this and it makes several conclusions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The question seems to be that two enclaves were unlawfully joined and he asked whether it was unlawful. I think the witness can answer the question as far as he can -- he knows. Mr. Groenewegen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to stick with the idea that I was only in the northern part of the enclave and that I cannot state anything about what happened in the southern part of the enclave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just one more question then. Do you agree that the operation of the Army of Republika Srpska in July 1995 began here, in the south, near Operation Post Echo marked by the letter E?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: The first information that we received about irregularities, OPs being attacked, did indeed come from the south as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The irregularities of attack against observation posts, were the observation posts themselves the targets or did the Army of Republika Srpska want to put them back in their place again and separate the enclaves?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: I cannot judge about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we then agree that you cannot be the judge of other things either. You can tell us only about things you knew and saw, and concerning observation posts and attacks on them, your statement contains a lot of inferences and allegations that are based on the conclusions you made, not on what you saw?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you be more specific, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Groenewegen states his conclusions. He qualifies military formations and speaks about the intentions of the Army of Republika Srpska that he couldn't know about and he wasn't even there where the attacks happened. He didn't see them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. -- I ask you to be specific in this issue, but point out some paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will, Your Excellency. I'll be happy when we come to that, but I will suggest that we consider whether each of his particular statements is an inference or direct knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, you did not see many armed people in Srebrenica, did you, and in no case did you ever seize a weapon from somebody?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Well, to that question I can answer: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Also, you did not see or you didn't know -- but did you perhaps hear of the military operations of Muslim forces from Srebrenica launched from the enclave, outside the enclave, against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Quite honestly, I don't recall any of that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you aware of the mandate of military observers and did you notice their presence in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Not as far as I know, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In that case it would not be correct to say, would it, that military observers mediated between you and the Serbs, that on your behalf they asked for safe passage or provided escort to you?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Objection. He cannot answer that question. He just -- I ask that it be withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We heard a Prosecution witness who portrayed the role of two military observers in a very grand manner. I am now questioning a witness who was supposed to enjoy the services of these military observers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just put your question whether he knew or not, instead of asking him whether it's correct or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know that military observers were taking care of you, they were asking permits for your safe movement on your behalf, and providing escort to your unit?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I must say -- I must ask again. Did you know that the Muslim forces made incursions into Serb villages and killed?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Not at that time. Later on when I was back in the Netherlands I heard about that, but that otherwise does not apply to the period I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we call 65 ter 16880, page 1. And then in that document page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a lady, Esther van Osselen. Do you know this lady?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: The name does not ring a bell.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You were quoted here: [In English] "The Dutch soldiers were anxious about the Muslim soldiers on the war path as much as they were about the Serbs. Paul Groenewegen (18) from Rotterdam: 'From our observation posts we saw with night vision equipment the Muslims leave the enclave mainly to smuggle stuff, but also to fight. The next day they talked tough about how they cut Chetniks' throats. These guys were stiff with cocaine, I can recognise that coming from Rotterdam.'" [Interpretation] What can you tell us about this? It seems that you had night vision, that you knew about this, and that you were able to observe nightly excursions of Muslims into Serb territory and you heard them brag how they slit Serb throats, the Chetniks' throats.

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: You're entirely right. I did not say this in those exact words. This was as a consequence of an interview in Assen and the words have been completely distorted.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see page 1 again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that this lady, Ms. Esther van Osselen, was reporting from Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: That she was reporting from Zagreb does not really ring a bell to me, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it true what it says in line 5 -- sorry, paragraph 5, where you say that a Muslim soldier turned around, Bosnian Serbs turned him face to the wall and pointed a gun at his head? Did you really tell her that or did she somehow make it up?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Well, of course it's not true that she made it up, but as for it having been conveyed in these words, I certainly cannot confirm that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you remember seeing that news article? Why don't you show him the last page of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Have you ever seen this in a Dutch newspaper?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: I never saw this, no. At one point I saw an article on a front page and the words used there were not mine either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did this lady, Esther, record your interview? And if we asked her, do you think she could give us the recording? Do you remember speaking into a microphone?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: No, I couldn't say anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What we see on the front page about killing a Muslim soldier is not something she made up. You told her that, and from that we must infer that you also told her what she wrote on page 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. You can ask what did the witness tell the journalist since he answered that -- let me find the passage. He said: "I did not say this in those exact words. This was as a consequence of an interview in Assen ..." So do you remember what you told the journalist as to the incident what you allegedly saw at your OP at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, what I told her corresponds with what I've stated here earlier. But I was also frustrated at seeing the serious distortion of my words conveyed in the newspaper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you remember what you told the lady as to the alleged smuggling or the attack from within to outside?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it was said that that type of information reached us, but I never used the terms as reflected in the newspaper. Apparently she changed my statement about the fact that we heard it into reading that I knew that and had actually seen it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I note the time now. It's time to take a break. We will take a break for an hour and resume at 20 to 2.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.40 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For the remainder of today's session, we'll be sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis, with Judge Robinson -- I'm sorry, Judge Morrison unable to attend due to his urgent personal reasons. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Excellencies, may I tender the first and the third pages of this paper, the interview which in the witness's words are his words but manipulated, as he said?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. In regard to this article the witness said: I did not say that in those exact words, I never saw this, those words have been completely distorted. And as having for it being conveyed in those words, I certainly cannot confirm that. The witness's comments about this article bear on its reliability. In addition, when you go to the end of the article itself, it indicates that the last column of the text is cut off, so it's not even the full article. And I would submit that it's not reliable for the Chamber to accept and I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: But, Ms. West, but did he not say that she did not make this up?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: She's -- yes, he did, in regard to the execution that is cited in here, the subject matter of that. But by indicating that these are not his words -- and he's indicated it four exact times, I would say that that calls into question the reliability of the article itself because we can't be sure that what is exactly conveyed is the truth. But yes, he did say that the incident itself did happen but not in this way. And I would submit that you can't rely on this being a reliable document without the journalist herself coming in here and saying: That's exactly what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: If I could just be heard briefly on this point. The witness did acknowledge speaking with the reporter and about the topics which is covered by the article. I think the remainder of it will go to weight, whether or not what she has recorded or reported was exactly what he said or distorted in some way should go to the weight but not to the admissibility. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll mark it for identification. So we'll -- but we'll come back to this issue. We'll rule on this issue as soon as practicable when Judge Morrison comes back.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: MFI D2003, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Page 1 and 3 as well as page 5, which is an actual clipping of Dutch newspaper. We'll mark it for identification. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Groenewegen, I'm a little nonplussed. Do you know about a book written by Mr. or Mrs. Praamsma containing interviews with over a hundred DutchBat members? It's a Dutch book and the author took statements from many DutchBat soldiers, including you?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: I know that a book was compiled of that, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D04720 is the next document I would like to call up in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a provisional translation into English made by my team from Dutch. Do you know this man, Frans van Rossum?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: No, he was not a direct co-worker of mine.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the second page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you please look at paragraph 2 where he describes the moment when the Muslims threw a grenade on a DutchBat APC killing Soldier van Renssen. Have you ever heard about this?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: I've definitely heard something about that, but I'm not aware of all the substantive details.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm sorry to interrupt. May I just be heard? We've looked at this document. I understand it's a book. The book does not exist in this building. The book I think is only in Dutch and so this translation is just -- looks like paragraphs from particular pages. So there's no way for me to look at this and see if any of this is taken out of context at all. I cannot at all respond to any questions based on this book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Were you not provided with any copy of Dutch book itself?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We were provided with this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: -- this English translation and that's it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, whenever I need something from the Prosecution, I have to -- I'm left to my own devices. They are in a much better position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, you should tender the Dutch original version as well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They received it. They received it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Well, I think -- I think he must have the Dutch and show him the Dutch. What I'm saying is, though, I don't have a full English in context so I can't -- I don't know what comes before and after any of this. But if he has the Dutch, maybe the witness should see the Dutch.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, no, have you received the Dutch version?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We've received the Dutch version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But not the --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Of these particular cites, of these particular English cites.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, let us see how -- where we can go. Let us continue. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Groenewegen, do you remember that it was a tragic event and a send-off was organised for the casket of this Dutch soldier when he was being sent home?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Take a look at this please. Did you know Lieutenant Arthur Batalona --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, let me pre-empt. I don't follow the exercise of putting this interview by third parties to the witness. Why don't you ask the question directly to the witness without having to tender this? You know the practice of not admitting third party's interview or articles unless the author confirms the content of the article. This is totally a waste of time. Why don't you just put your question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: My question is: Please look at the words of Sergeant Arthur Batalona about the excursions of Muslim fighters and the slaughter of Serbs, which is consistent with your words as reported by that lady, Esther. Look at the first paragraph, please. Does this conform with what you knew and what you told that lady, Esther?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Well, a certain similarity is perceptible, but once again all the facts that I told here, I was informed of them only after my deployment. So I think that facts are being confused here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. We'll come to that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the next page, please. It begins here at the bottom, the words of the Sergeant Alvin van Hecke, and what he says concerns your observation post. The first paragraph says that by night, they went out to Serb territory, burnt and killed, and then returned and hid behind your positions.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, just -- I don't know if the witness has the English or the Dutch in front of him. Maybe we should inquire whether he wants --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think he's following his e-court but --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May we inquire if he would be more comfortable with the Dutch.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But before that I -- did you understand my point, Mr. Karadzic? I said there's no point of putting these questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The reason will become clear soon. Mr. Groenewegen was connected with Observation Post Mike where this was happening. This man was from the same observation post. Mr. Groenewegen told the same thing in his earlier statements but his later statements changed his version somewhat, and I want to question him about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just put that question to the witness, having said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Groenewegen, did Muslim soldiers leave the enclave by night, go to the Serb territory, and then returned, and did they place their trenches near your observation post and those trenches were naturally a target for the Serb army?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: The only subject I can make any statement about, in fact, is that trenches were indeed dug very close to our observation posts. The rest of that question is something I was told about by third parties much later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement dated 29 September 1995, 65 ter 19529; and also in your testimony in the Blagojevic case on the 10th of July, 2003, 65 ter 03237, did you state that carrying out your duties at OP Mike you saw the beginning of the Serb offensive and you saw Serb positions and you also saw shells falling, shells fired as a provocation by the Serb troops, at least that's how you experienced it. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, would I be right in saying that in the Blagojevic case, on page 1040, you understood the military reasoning behind it, and I'm going to paraphrase. [In English] "The shooting was to cut off a road to Potocari and keep the civilian population from -- the civilian population in the same place that they were." [Interpretation] So was your observation post hit or is it the case, as you stated in the Blagojevic case, that it was some kind of barrage fire to prevent movement?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: It would appear to me to be the latter because no actual targets of ours were hit. It would appear to have been purely a provocation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But here you said in your evidence, you said that it was what is known as barrage fire, fire that prevents others from moving about and is not intended to kill them. Right?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: The term "barrage fire," as reflected here in English is something that is unfamiliar to me. But the people did not want to move to any other place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, on the next page you say that they had moved towards Potocari, whereas you believed it would have been better for them to have stayed and to fight. [In English] "... it was better for them to fight than to head towards Potocari on a voluntarily basis." [Interpretation] Did you say that?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you locate it on this page?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: I don't see my exact words here as you just presented to me, indicating that in my view they should have stayed and engaged in the fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The first paragraph, Mr. Groenewegen. It's contained in the question and you confirmed in your answer, saying "that is correct."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you like to put the question, why don't you show him the exact passage in his statement and ask him what he meant, as Mr. Stojanovic did in this case.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [In English] "At one point you provided the following answer to the Prosecution. You said you had talked to one of them, having in mind members of the BH army, and that they told you allegedly that it was better for them to fight than to head towards Potocari on a voluntarily basis. Is that right?" And you said: "That is correct." [Interpretation] So you did meet with the Muslim troops, you spoke to one of them, and you deliberated whether it would have been better for them to stay and fight. It doesn't now matter who said what, but what's discussed here was leaving for Potocari on a voluntarily basis.

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: I've seen it and I understand now, and this comes across to me as their words that were presented to me. But I can't form an opinion about that, as to what would have been best for them to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You can look at the text up to line 15, the same issue is discussed. You had your opinion, they had theirs, and all of this indicates that they decided of their own free will to go to Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: There's no question there, Your Honour. It's just a statement.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I asked whether it's correct. [In English] But it's not in transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, could you please answer the question all at once about this matter.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Excuse me, could you please ask the question all at once about this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'll make it simpler. Is it true, as written here, that this Muslim soldier spoke to you about what would have been better for them, to stay and fight or to go to Potocari on a voluntarily basis?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll go back to that when I find your opinion about this voluntarily nature of their movement. To the best of your knowledge, who ordered the civilians to go to Potocari and who took the decision for the column of soldiers and civilians to break out towards Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: I can't state anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I should like to clarify what my learned friend Mrs. West also asked you. They did not come of their own free will. Then we have to make it more precise. Did they come of their own decision or somebody made the decision for them?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: I can't judge that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But this Defence has to understand. Did they come reluctantly or did they come against their will? If they came reluctantly, was it the situation that forced their hand or was it somebody that forced them?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Then that would be more likely to be the situation than that somebody actually ordered them. But once again, that's speculation on my part.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that the Muslim authorities sent their people to all villages to pass on the order that all the civilians must go to Potocari, whereas the fighting men should make a breakthrough?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm not getting any interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Groenewegen, could you repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course. I know nothing about that having happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have to get this out in the clear because the Prosecution is using the wording you used in the Blagojevic case as well. 65 ter 0323 [as interpreted]. This is the same page, 1041. Please put it back on. You say that you think they did not come to Potocari of their own free will. Do you mean to say that they were not happy to come or that they did not come of their own volition, that it was decided for them by someone else? Is that what you meant ?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: The only reason why I don't think they were there of their own volition is because those people were simply afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And look at what you said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, Mr. Karadzic, the witness said at line 25 he thought they had no other option, and it was confirmed when Ms. West asked the same question at the end of para 42 of his amalgamated statement. I think we've dealt with this question. Why don't you move on to your next topic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You deal with that in paragraph 19 of your statement as well. Is it correct that civilians, Muslim civilians, left their homes considerably before the Serb troops entered those same homes?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: I couldn't state anything about that. I don't have any more time perception about that period in the sense of how long or how short those events succeeded one another.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But can you confirm that when you dealt with part of the civilians, when you took them to Potocari, that the Serbs did not have any physical contact with the civilians who had set out to Potocari?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Just to be clear, he just said "when you took them to Potocari." I think that's a misstatement. Maybe he could just ask that question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Groenewegen, did you drive some people, some civilians, women and children, that is, to Potocari using UN vehicles?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: No. At that time I didn't even have a driver's licence. And in any case, I did not escort people to Potocari; they all came to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. When I say "you," I speak about the Dutch Battalion. I'm not referring to you personally. As a matter of fact, did the Dutch Battalion get instructions to help civilians reach Potocari?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: I don't know whether they were instructed to do so. From my position, I saw that at least one truck rode toward Potocari filled with refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please look at page 1020 in 65 ter 03237 and then page 1020. This is what you say: "Most of these individuals arrived on foot, whereas some were brought in on trucks, vehicles of the UN." In paragraph 19 you say that they were all making a valiant effort to get to Potocari.

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: I don't remember the words "valiant."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 19 of your amalgamated statement. However, let us deal first with this page 1020. It says: [In English] "Were they primarily on foot or were they being transported some other way?" From the beginning, from line 1. Your answer: "The majority did. Others had been brought to the bases by UN vehicles." [Interpretation] Now this is what I'm asking you: Before they were taken onto UN vehicles and before they set out on foot, did they have any physical contact with the Army of Republika Srpska? Was it the Army of Republika Srpska that had expelled them out of their homes?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think this witness has made this clear several times, that he was not in a position to answer this question. He's on the receiving end in Potocari. So he has no ability to answer the questions about the people leaving Potocari only upon their arriving and he said this several times.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I disagree, Excellency. I asked whether the United Nations transported these people, and in the testimony here it says "yes." And not in a single vehicle but the word is used in the plural, it says "vehicles."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Since the witness gave evidence to the effect that they didn't leave on their own free will and that they were really fearful, albeit repetitive, I think that can be asked. Just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But it is truly repetitive. Can you answer the question, Mr. Groenewegen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In any case, I know that they arrived on foot at the compound from Potocari and I was there to escort the people through the gate rather than along the side paths. That was my task on site. And I saw a few but I actually remember one truck filled with people arriving at the Potocari compound. And I can't say anything else about their movements than I said earlier. The people were frightened even about receiving security from DutchBat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you have five minutes to conclude.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, I kindly ask that I be given the rest of the session, if for no other reason for the waste of time involving interpretation into three languages, Dutch, English, Serbian. We are losing a lot of time that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, in order for you to concentrate on relevant and important issues, the Chamber is not minded to extend your cross-examination, the time for cross-examination of this witness, further.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, it is very important for me what it means "of their own free will." Did they come happily? Gladly? Or not? But whose decision was it? Because the accusation is that the Serbs forcefully expelled --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, the Chamber believes that it has allowed you sufficient time to cover all the issues, but it's up to you how you would spend the time allotted. You have five minutes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With all due respect, Excellencies, the indictment and many judgements say that civilians from Srebrenica were expelled by the Serbs. The key moment is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you have an opportunity to present your submission, but it's time for you to ask the questions to this witness which the witness is able to answer. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. Mr. Groenewegen, is it correct that those who had allegedly killed that man afterwards hid in the bushes?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Yes, they ran away after that, and I'm not sure where they went.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. Is it correct that you saw men in the white house; and if so, how many? You don't know that it was called the white house but you know what I'm referring to. How many were there approximately, 200? 300?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: It could never have been that many all at once, given what I remember about the house. But I do know that men were placed in there multiple times and subsequently transported away.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the Popovic case you said something that was changed later in your new statement. You said there on 1D04738 on page 282, or rather, 2980, that -- you said that all refugees wanted to go towards the buses. Later on you said that some people were forced by Serb soldiers to board buses. Now I want us to take a look at that. Does this confusion not come from the fact that there were refugees who wanted to board the buses and there were men, on the other hand, that Serbs treated as prisoners of war? Did they force those men to board the buses?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: No. From what I remember, the last people, or rather, the women and children were also basically forced to board the buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But how do we reconcile that with what you said in the Popovic case? Also, on the film we see that all of those who wanted to leave, leave in peace and there is no force involved.

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: I can't give you an answer to that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On one occasion you said that Serbs took away your rifle and on another occasion you said that nothing was taken away from you. What is correct? I don't have time to give you an actual reference. Did you once say that you had your things taken away from you and did you say on another occasion that nothing was taken away from you?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: All I remember is that I stated that my weapon was taken from me. I don't remember stating that nothing was taken from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Until we find the reference, is it correct that you stated in the Popovic case -- no, Tolimir, you stated that your task was to enable those who wanted to board the buses to do so and that there were two groups: One group that wanted to do that and others who did not?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the amalgamated statement, paragraph 8, you say: [In English] "All the refugees, everybody wanted to go toward the buses." [Interpretation] Do you make a distinction between refugees and those who were in the house and that Serbs were treating differently, not to say as prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: That's perfectly possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you state that you did not find out that any one of the Muslims wanted to remain in Srebrenica? You said that in the Tolimir case in April last year -- the year before last, that is. 1D04737. On page 1198. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's somewhere around line 2.

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: From my perception, the majority of people did want to board the buses right away, and later on the people who hesitated were mildly forced to board the buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at lines 16 through 18. [In English] "My next question: Did you ever hear from anybody, through an interpreter or personally, that some of the Muslims who had gathered in Potocari requested to stay in Srebrenica?" [Interpretation] Your answer: [In English] "Not as far as I know." [Interpretation] Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: Not as far as I know in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. 1D4739, page 3, you say that you had your rifle taken away from you, and in 65 ter 19P29 [as interpreted], on page 8753 you say that nothing was ever taken away from you. What is correct out of all of this and why does it differ?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, let us upload the second thing. What is the 65 ter number?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 19P29 [as interpreted], and then page 8753.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Check the number again.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It should be correct. Statement in September 1995. Perhaps it's the wrong page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably 19529.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what I said, yes. Now this page, 7853 [as interpreted], what we've already said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Page 4.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it's page 4 in the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The second-last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [In English] "The BSA took nothing from me."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. I see the source of confusion. The version where I stated that my rifle was taken is the correct version and it is very strange to me that this appears here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us, is it correct that you did not see any mosque being hit or any other such facility?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: No, I don't recall anything about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now it's time to put your last question, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, for the transcript and with all due respect, even if one were not to take into account the loss of time involving interpretation into three languages, this is not enough time to cross-examine the witness. There are so many contradictions and there are so many opportunities for the Defence to have a completely different picture painted that I have to say that I am completely dissatisfied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm of a different opinion, Mr. Karadzic. Your last question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I kindly ask for one second, please, so that I can make a choice.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that you said that you did not see refugees handing over their property, their belongings?

utterances.speaker: PAUL GROENEWEGEN
utterances.text: I did not see anything like that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That is also in this statement on page 00438752.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If that's it, if I cannot deal with anything else, that will be my last question, however, with me saying that I do not consider this witness to have been cross-examined.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's not acceptable, Mr. Karadzic. Ms. West, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Groenewegen, on behalf of the Chamber --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I? I beg your pardon, Your Excellency. May I tender at least these pages from this statement from 1995, the ones that I have displayed and where I quoted from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That statement is only of five pages. Why don't we admit it in its entirety then?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it there's no objection from the Prosecution? 19529 will be admitted as Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2004, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you again, Mr. Groenewegen, for your coming to the Tribunal again to give it. Now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we proceed with the next witness? Please call your next witness, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I call Roger Patelski, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. While the next witness is being brought in, I would like to deal with this matter. The Chamber is seized of the accused's motion to reclassify response to invitation to United Kingdom filed on 10th of January, 2012. The Chamber finds that there's nothing in the response from the UK that requires it to remain confidential and thus grants the accused's motion. The Chamber hereby directs the Registry to reclassify as public the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland's response to the Trial Chamber's order of 17 November inviting submissions filed on 5 January 2012.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Could you kindly take the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I state that I will tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please make yourself comfortable. Yes, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May we have 65 ter 90302, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: ROGER PATELSKI
utterances.text: Hello.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: What is your name?

utterances.speaker: ROGER PATELSKI
utterances.text: My name is Roger Felix Theodora Bernardus Patelski.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: What is your current rank?

utterances.speaker: ROGER PATELSKI
utterances.text: I'm presently a sergeant first class.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: What is your current post in the military?

utterances.speaker: ROGER PATELSKI
utterances.text: I'm presently stationed at the 13th Battalion of the infantry battalion mobile in Assen.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, an amalgamated statement was prepared containing relevant portions of your OTP statement from 2000 and information you provided in October of 2011. This statement on the screen now, is this the one you reviewed and signed on November 30th, 2011?

utterances.speaker: ROGER PATELSKI
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And just for the record, you also have a hard copy right next to you of the same statement. Can you confirm that the statement accurately reflects an amalgamation of your previous 2000 statement and the information that you recently provided?

utterances.speaker: ROGER PATELSKI
utterances.text: That's also entirely correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, if you were asked today about the same matters contained in the statement, would you provide the same information to the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: ROGER PATELSKI
utterances.text: I would still provide the same information, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, we tender the statement. There are no associated exhibits; however, on the table of additional exhibits we asked to use there are two maps in which I requested 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are there any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The statement will be admitted as Exhibit P -- shall we give the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P4173, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And your request for leave is granted.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may summarise the statement. Mr. Patelski is currently in the Royal Netherlands Army. In 1995 he was a private stationed at the Potocari compound. In June of 1995 he was posted to Observation Post P, known as OP Papa, situated about 1 kilometre north of the main entrance of the compound. Patelski's duties included patrolling the area to monitor suspicious activity, speaking with people in and around the compound, and escorting UNHCR convoys bringing in supplies. By that time the Serbs were blocking many of the trucks from entering the compound, and without food, water, or gas, conditions had severely deteriorated in Srebrenica for both the civilian population and DutchBat soldiers, who were forced to patrol on foot as they did not have sufficient fuel for their vehicles. The Serbian military post called Yellow Bridge was located half a kilometre further north. Patelski spoke with Jovo, the commander of that post. During Patelski's prior posting to OP Papa which was between February and March 1995, Jovo had informed Patelski that the Serbs were going to attack the enclave. About two weeks before the fall of the enclave, Patelski noticed that Serb troops were building up their presence around the compound. Before the offensive attack in July, he saw Serb military movements in the hills above Potocari. He also saw the Serbs digging trenches and setting up rocket-launchers and mortars around the enclave. They used the latter to shoot at Muslim houses while Serb snipers shot at civilians, including older men, women and children. The injured were then brought to the DutchBat compound for treatment. On July 11th, Patelski heard on the radio that Serbian troops had taken the Srebrenica enclave from the south. The next day, the 12th, the Serbian troops around OP Papa began advancing in the direction of Potocari. Jovo called OP Papa and informed the DutchBat soldiers that if they did not resist, they would not be harmed.
